avoid: fake science or unsupported 'clinically proven' claims

plan.summary: Budget leans to Studiogrid, where a just-booked yoga or training session is a direct trigger for buying activewear, with tests on sustainability-receptive audiences (Stride & Stem, Pantrygood) and fitness-adjacent supplements (Daily Form); activewear sellers and mid-life conservative womenswear are excluded.

recommended.name: Studiogrid

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 74% female; high income for premium price

recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a generic wellness-audience match and capped it at test, but the purchase itself is the connection: a shopper who just booked a yoga class or personal training session needs something to wear to it, and the notes confirm they are mid-transaction on fitness spend at high income.
recommended.rationale: Booking a fitness class or personal training session is the single clearest trigger for buying leggings, and the notes say these shoppers are 'actively spending on self-care and fitness' at high income with a 74% female skew.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

recommended.risk: $85 is roughly 2x the $42 class booking, so the offer is a bigger commitment than the purchase that preceded it; sustainability messaging may matter less here than fit and performance.

test.name: Stride & Stem

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 94% female; high income for premium price

test.rationale: A 94%-female, high-income base where the notes say 'Sustainability and machine-washable claims resonate' is the right ear for a recycled-ocean-plastic pitch, and at $142 typical spend the $85 offer is easy; the open question is whether professional-shoe buyers are also gym buyers.

evidence.quote: Professional women. Sustainability and machine-washable claims resonate

test.risk: Workwear-shoe intent is not workout intent, and 3.2M impressions gives a thin read on a test.

test.name: Pantrygood

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 71% female; high income for premium price

test.rationale: Notes describe shoppers 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' at $86 baskets, so the recycled-ocean-plastic story should land; what needs measuring is whether values alignment converts without any activewear intent.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: A pantry restock is a routine grocery moment, not a wardrobe moment; sustainability affinity may not translate into an $85 apparel purchase.

test.name: Daily Form

signals.name: audience
signals.detail: 89% female; mid-high income for premium price

test.rationale: An 89%-female, 22-42 supplement buyer is usually training for something, making activewear a plausible next purchase; the uncertainty is a $38 basket absorbing an $85 offer and a readership the notes call skeptical of thin claims.

evidence.quote: Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims

test.risk: $85 is 2.2x the typical order at mid-high income, and 'recycled ocean plastic' needs substantiation for an audience trained to interrogate claims.

campaign.name: Sustainable women's activewear made from recycled ocean plastic · post-purchase launch

bid_strategy.rationale: $85 first order × 0.30 = $25.50 target CPA: one-time purchase, so the first order has to pay back the acquisition. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

test_plan.hypothesis: A 94%-female, high-income base where the notes say 'Sustainability and machine-washable claims resonate' is the right ear for a recycled-ocean-plastic pitch, and at $142 typical spend the $85 offer is easy; the open question is whether professional-shoe buyers are also gym buyers.
test_plan.risk: Workwear-shoe intent is not workout intent, and 3.2M impressions gives a thin read on a test.

launch_summary.summary: $8,500 of the $10,000 goes to Studiogrid, where a just-booked yoga or training session makes activewear the obvious next buy. The remaining $1,500 is split evenly across three tests: Stride & Stem and Pantrygood to see whether sustainability-minded shoppers convert without workout intent, and Daily Form to see whether supplement buyers will stretch to an $85 apparel order. Target cost per new customer is $25.50, with $33.15 as the ceiling during the 14-day learning period.
uncertainties: The $85 first order is inferred from price positioning, and both the $25.50 target and $33.15 maximum are built on it rather than on real margin or repeat value.
The plan assumes one-time purchases, so the first order must pay back acquisition entirely; a subscription or strong repeat rate would change what's affordable.
The ad written for The Affluent Classic won't run at all, since no placement's shoppers fit that persona.
